topic.angle: What the effect does and does not say

body.claim: The Dunning-Kruger effect does not show that unskilled people rate themselves above experts.
body.why: In the classic exam data, low performers overestimated their abilities, but their self-assessment was still lower than that of high performers. Laypeople often misread it as saying low-intelligence people are more confident than high-intelligence people. Some critics argue the pattern may largely be a statistical effect, plus a general tendency to think we are better than average.

probes.question: True or false: in the classic data, low performers rated themselves higher than high performers did.
What does the statistical explanation say about the effect?
options: It may largely be a mere statistical effect
It proves poor performers cannot learn

claims.claim: Effect does not claim low performers are as confident as high performers
claims.quote: Nor does it claim that people lacking a given skill are as confident as high performers.

claims.claim: Low performers overestimated but self-assessment was still lower than high performers (probe 1)
claims.quote: Nevertheless, low performers' self-assessment is lower than that of high performers.

claims.claim: Low performers overestimated their abilities in the exam data
claims.quote: the participants who scored in the bottom quartile overestimated their test performance and their abilities

claims.claim: Laypeople misread it as low-intelligence people being more confident than high-intelligence people
claims.quote: Among laypeople, the Dunning-Kruger effect is often misunderstood as the claim that people with low intelligence are more confident in their knowledge

claims.claim: Critics: pattern may largely be a statistical effect (probe 2)
claims.quote: the empirical effect may largely be the result of a mere statistical effect

claims.claim: ...plus a general tendency to think we are better than average
claims.quote: people have a general tendency to think that they are better than average
